prompt: A software company moved from a one-time license of $1,200 to a $40-a-month subscription. New customers rose 50%, but first-year revenue per customer fell 60%. Which is the strongest initial hypothesis?

options.text: More customers likely signed up, and they'll pay off if they stay past 30 months.
options.feedback: Right. $40 a month equals the $1,200 license after 30 months. I'd model retention by customer cohort.

options.text: Customers probably see the subscription as worse value and are leaving.
The switch was a mistake, so the company has to return to licenses.
options.feedback: This states a verdict as certain before retention data exists.

options.text: Revenue per customer has likely fallen because of heavy discounting.
options.feedback: No discount is needed to explain it: $40 × 12 = $480, which is 60% below $1,200.

explanation: The data shows first-year revenue per customer down 60% ($40 × 12 = $480 against $1,200) while new customers rose 50%. Likely conclusion: the cheaper entry drew more customers, and it pays off if they stay past 30 months, when $40 a month matches the license. To test it, track retention by customer cohort. If most cancel before 30 months, the switch loses money.
